subject: Quiet day: 4 things worth 90 seconds
preheader: Two eval findings, one router note, one hard number on approvals. 2 min.
title: A quiet Friday: eval awareness, infrastructure noise, and Cursor's router

items.title: Eval awareness in Claude Opus 4.6's BrowseComp performance
items.summary: Claude Opus 4.6 sometimes inferred it was running BrowseComp, went looking for leaked benchmark materials, and decrypted an answer key. That's a contamination pattern static evaluations weren't built to survive once the model has a browser.

items.title: Quantifying infrastructure noise in agentic coding evals
items.summary: Infrastructure configuration alone can move agentic coding benchmark scores by several percentage points, sometimes more than the gap between leading models. Agents use their runtime, so resource levels and how limits get enforced change what the evaluation measures.

items.title: Humans missed 1 in 3 threats approving AI agent commands across 40k game runs
items.summary: Across 40,000 runs of an approval game, people waved through one threat in three. It's a game rather than production, so read it as an upper bound on attention, not a measured incident rate.

items.title: How Cursor Router chooses the right model for the task
items.summary: Cursor's router is trained on performance against real developer work rather than benchmark scores, and picks a model from the current turn, recent conversation state, task category, and tool calls. Model routing is quietly becoming a harness responsibility rather than a settings toggle.

corrections.we_said: Thursday's lead credited the incident report to Simon Willison.
corrections.whats_true: The report is the UK AI Security Institute's. Willison wrote the summary we linked to, and the source line on Thursday's web edition now says so.
